terms.definition: A fixed-length value produced by running an algorithm over every byte of a file. Any change to even one byte produces a completely different output — making data corruption impossible to hide.
terms.example: The SHA-256 checksum of image.jpg is OI5plY1Is6EKEzQl...T8= — if even one pixel changes, this value becomes completely different

terms.definition: Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit — a cryptographic hash function producing a 256-bit output. Provides the strongest security among S3 checksum options. Preferred for compliance-sensitive environments (HIPAA, PCI-DSS).
terms.example: Used for medical imaging archives, financial records, and any data requiring cryptographic proof of integrity

terms.definition: Cyclic Redundancy Check Castagnoli — a 32-bit error-detecting algorithm optimized for hardware acceleration in modern CPUs and SSDs. The fastest S3 checksum option. Not cryptographic.
terms.example: Recommended for high-throughput media upload pipelines processing terabytes daily where performance matters more than cryptographic strength

terms.definition: Cyclic Redundancy Check (32-bit) — a fast error-detecting algorithm. Slightly slower than CRC32-C but widely supported. Not a cryptographic algorithm.
terms.example: Suitable for general media uploads and non-regulated data where quick integrity detection is needed

terms.definition: Secure Hash Algorithm 160-bit — produces a 160-bit output. Considered cryptographically weak today (collision vulnerabilities known). Supported for legacy compatibility only.
terms.example: Only use for systems that already have SHA-1 baked in and cannot be updated — not for new implementations

terms.definition: A method of encoding binary data as ASCII text using 64 characters. Amazon S3 stores and displays checksum values in base64 format. The shasum command outputs hex, which must be converted.
terms.example: Hex value '3894a5ff...' becomes 'OI5p...' in base64 — the xxd -r -p | base64 pipeline performs this conversion

terms.definition: A guarantee that data is verified both at upload AND at download, covering the complete lifecycle. The checksum established at upload is the baseline, validated again at retrieval.
terms.example: S3 checksums are truly end-to-end: calculated at upload → stored with object → validated at download

terms.definition: A checksum value you calculate yourself before uploading and provide to S3 in the upload request. S3 rejects the upload if its own calculation differs — catching corruption at the point of entry.
terms.example: Calculate SHA-256 before upload, pass as --checksum-sha256 in CLI. If transfer corrupts even one byte, S3 rejects the upload immediately

terms.definition: The low-level AWS CLI command that maps directly to the S3 REST PutObject API. Supports full checksum control via --checksum-algorithm and --checksum-sha256, unlike the high-level aws s3 cp command.
terms.example: aws s3api put-object --bucket B --key K --body file.jpg --checksum-algorithm SHA256

terms.definition: AWS CLI command that retrieves object metadata WITHOUT downloading the file data. Returns content type, size, ETag, ChecksumSHA256, ReplicationStatus, and other metadata. Essential for at-scale integrity validation.
terms.example: aws s3api head-object --bucket B --key K --query ChecksumSHA256 --output text returns just the checksum value

terms.definition: An S3 feature that preserves multiple versions of every object. When an object is deleted or overwritten, all previous versions are retained and can be restored. Essential for backup systems.
terms.example: Uploading project-report.txt three times creates Version 1, 2, and 3. Delete adds a delete marker — all three versions still exist and are recoverable

terms.definition: A special version created in a versioned S3 bucket when an object is deleted. Makes the object appear gone to standard requests but all actual versions remain. Removing the delete marker restores the object.
terms.example: aws s3 rm on a versioned object creates a delete marker. The object reappears immediately when the marker is removed

terms.definition: An S3 feature that automatically copies objects from a source bucket to a destination bucket in a different AWS region. Requires versioning on both buckets and an IAM replication role.
terms.example: Primary bucket in us-east-1 automatically replicates to secondary bucket in us-west-2 for disaster recovery — checksums are preserved in the replica

terms.definition: An S3 object metadata field showing the current state of cross-region replication: PENDING (queued), COMPLETED (success), FAILED (error — check IAM), or REPLICA (this is the destination copy).
terms.example: aws s3api head-object --query ReplicationStatus returns COMPLETED for successfully replicated objects

terms.definition: An S3 feature that prevents objects from being deleted or modified for a defined retention period (WORM — Write Once Read Many). Required for compliance with regulations like HIPAA, SEC, FINRA that mandate immutable records.
terms.example: Combined with SHA-256 checksums, Object Lock provides cryptographic proof of integrity AND immutability — the enterprise backup gold standard

terms.definition: An AWS IAM role that S3 assumes to perform cross-region replication. Requires specific permissions: s3:GetObjectVersionForReplication on source, s3:ReplicateObject on destination.
terms.example: If replication shows FAILED status, check that the IAM role has s3:ReplicateObject permission on the destination bucket ARN

terms.definition: S3's default integrity mechanism — typically the MD5 hash of an object, used for HTTP caching and conditional requests. For multipart uploads, the ETag is a composite value (not a simple MD5), making it unreliable for manual integrity verification.
terms.example: ETags look like d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e. For multipart uploads, they look like abc123-5 (hash-partcount) — not the file's MD5

terms.definition: S3 feature that splits large files into parts, uploads them (potentially in parallel), then assembles the final object. Required for files over 5GB. Each part can have its own checksum, plus a composite checksum covers the whole object.
terms.example: A 10GB video split into 100 × 100MB parts. Each part is checksum-verified independently — a single corrupted part requires re-uploading only that part

terms.definition: An S3 feature that guarantees 99.99% of objects replicate within 15 minutes. Includes CloudWatch metrics for monitoring replication delays and SLA metrics. More expensive than standard CRR.
terms.example: Use RTC when your DR strategy requires a guaranteed RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — standard CRR has no SLA on replication timing

terms.definition: AWS's fully managed immutable ledger database. Records cannot be deleted or modified — even by AWS administrators. Used to store checksums as an independent tamper-evident audit trail alongside S3 Object Lock.
terms.example: Store SHA-256 checksums in QLDB at upload time. Auditors can verify QLDB records independently of S3, proving no tampering even at the metadata level

terms.definition: A property of cryptographic hash functions where a tiny input change produces a completely different output. SHA-256 exhibits this — even adding one byte to a file changes all 256 bits of the hash unpredictably.
terms.example: Adding 'corruption' to a file changes its SHA-256 from OI5plY...T8= to something completely unrecognizable — no partial match, total change

terms.definition: A managed AWS service for large-scale data transfer that automatically handles checksum verification, retries, bandwidth throttling, and transfer reporting. The enterprise alternative to writing custom batch validation scripts.
terms.example: DataSync can transfer 10TB from an on-premises NAS to S3 overnight with built-in SHA-256 integrity checking — no custom scripts needed

terms.definition: A time-limited URL generated by an AWS principal that grants temporary upload or download access to a specific S3 object without requiring the recipient to have AWS credentials. Can be generated with checksum enforcement.
terms.example: A web app backend generates a pre-signed PUT URL with ChecksumAlgorithm=SHA256. The browser calculates the file checksum and uploads directly to S3 — S3 validates the checksum without the file touching the backend server

terms.definition: An AWS service that records every API call made to AWS services as structured JSON events, including who made the call, what parameters were passed, and when it happened. For S3, Data Events must be explicitly enabled to capture PutObject and GetObject calls.
terms.example: CloudTrail shows that a PutObject call at 3:47 AM used --checksum-algorithm SHA256 and came from IAM user backup-agent — providing a complete audit trail of every upload

terms.definition: An S3 feature that generates scheduled flat-file reports (CSV or Parquet) listing every object in a bucket with metadata including checksum algorithm, checksum type, ETag, size, and storage class. Delivered to a destination bucket for querying with Athena.
terms.example: A daily Inventory report for a 10-million-object archive bucket enables Athena queries to find all objects missing checksums or using SHA-1 instead of SHA-256 — without calling head-object 10 million times

terms.definition: The checksum S3 stores for a multipart upload object. It is NOT the SHA-256 of the assembled file — it is SHA-256 of the concatenated base64 part checksums. Cannot be reproduced by running sha256sum on the local file.
terms.example: A 10-part upload has part checksums P1...P10. The composite is sha256(base64(P1) + base64(P2) + ... + base64(P10)) — completely different from sha256(whole-file)

terms.definition: An S3 feature that sends messages to SNS, SQS, or Lambda functions when specific events occur in a bucket — such as ObjectCreated, ObjectRemoved, or ObjectRestore. Used to trigger real-time processing of newly uploaded objects.
terms.example: S3 Event Notification triggers a Lambda function within seconds of every upload. Lambda calls headObject, compares checksum against DynamoDB baseline, and publishes to SNS if FAIL — real-time integrity monitoring

terms.definition: An S3 API operation that returns specific attributes of an object (Checksum, ETag, ObjectParts, ObjectSize, StorageClass) without downloading the object data. More efficient than headObject for checksum-only retrieval at large scale.
terms.example: lambda.getObjectAttributes({ Bucket, Key, ObjectAttributes: ['Checksum'] }) returns just the checksum data — 70% less response payload than headObject for checksum-only Lambda validation functions
